title: 7. Conditionals, Hedging & Hypothetical Reasoning
group: Module 2 · Band 7.0+ Complex Structures & Range Booster
blocks: The four conditionals as a scale of reality, the first-vs-second choice that matters most in Task 2, the one rule that removes most conditional errors, and the hedging toolkit for academic caution.

Conditionals let you argue about possibilities: what happens if something is true, what would happen if it were, and what would have happened if the past had been different. This is the grammar of consequence and hypothesis, and it is central to Task 2, where almost every argument is really a conditional in disguise: if governments do X, then Y will follow. Alongside conditionals sits hedging, the language of caution (may, tend to, it is likely that), which stops your claims from sounding absolute and makes your writing sound measured and academic.

Every conditional has an if-clause (the condition) and a main clause (the result). The order is free; if the if-clause comes first, it is followed by a comma. If demand rises, prices increase. = Prices increase if demand rises. The four standard conditionals differ only in the tense pattern across those two clauses, and each expresses a different degree of reality.
If you heat ice, it melts.
If taxes rise, consumption will fall.
If I were rich, I would fund schools.
If they had invested, the crisis would have been avoided.

Read the table as a scale of reality: zero is always true, first is realistically possible, second is imagined or unlikely, third is impossible now because the moment has passed. Choosing the right one is choosing how real you want the claim to sound.
A note on “were” in the second conditional: formal English uses were for all subjects (“If the government were to act …”), and this is the safer choice in Writing.
7.3 First versus second: the choice that matters most in Task 2
Most of your conditional errors and choices come down to first versus second, so drill this pair.
Use the first conditional for a real proposal you think is genuinely possible. If the government invests in public transport, congestion will decrease.
Use the second conditional for a hypothetical or a suggestion you are framing as imagined. If every citizen planted a tree, the city would be greener.
If the government will raise taxes, spending falls.
If the government raises taxes, spending will fall.
The if-clause of a first conditional takes the present simple, never “will.”
If I would be in charge, I would ban cars.
If I were in charge, I would ban cars.
The if-clause of a second conditional takes the past simple / “were,” never “would.”
The one rule that removes most conditional errors

Never put “will” or “would” in the if-clause. “Will” and “would” live in the result clause only. Keep the if-clause in a simple/past tense and you eliminate the most common conditional mistake in a single move.
7.4 Mixed and inverted conditionals (a Band 8+ touch)
Two advanced moves add range when they fit naturally:
Mixed conditional: a past condition with a present result. If they had planned better (past), the city would not be so congested now (present).
Inverted conditional (formal, drops “if”): Had the government acted sooner, the crisis would have been avoided. = If the government had acted sooner … (You will meet inversion fully in Chapter 8.)
Use these once, accurately, for effect. A forced mixed conditional is worse than a clean standard one.
7.5 Hedging: the language of academic caution

Hedging means softening a claim so it is not an absolute statement. Band 5 writing is full of overstatements (always, never, everyone, will definitely). Band 8 writing qualifies its claims, which paradoxically makes them sound more credible and more academic. This is one of the fastest ways to raise the maturity of your tone.
tend to, be likely to, appear to, seem to
often, generally, in many cases, to some extent, relatively
it is likely that, it appears that, there is a tendency for
many, some, a significant number of, the majority of
Junk food always causes obesity and will destroy public health.
Excessive consumption of junk food may contribute to obesity and could place a strain on public health.
“always causes” and “will destroy” are overstated; “may contribute” and “could place a strain” are measured.

Hedging is not weakness or vagueness. It is precision about how certain you are. “Immigration boosts the economy” is a claim you cannot fully prove; “Immigration can boost the economy” is one you can defend.

Two clusters of error dominate. The first is tense leakage in conditionals (putting will/would in the if-clause). The second is the habit of writing sweeping absolutes, which comes partly from the strength of assertion common in Bangla essay style.

Error type 1 · “will/would” in the if-clause.
✗ If the price will increase, demand will fall. / If governments would ban plastic, pollution would drop.
✓ If the price increases, demand will fall. / If governments banned plastic, pollution would drop.

Error type 2 · Unqualified absolutes.
✗ Technology always improves our lives. / Every student prefers online classes.
✓ Technology generally improves our lives. / Many students appear to prefer online classes.
Conditionals and hedging together define Task 2 maturity

Task 2 rewards two things this chapter delivers. Conditionals give you the structure to argue consequences (“if this policy is adopted, then …”), which is the backbone of a body paragraph. Hedging gives you the tone to make those arguments sound reasoned rather than dogmatic. A script that combines an accurate second conditional with well-placed hedging reads as clearly Band 7-plus, because it shows both grammatical range and rhetorical control.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Task 2 (first conditional): If governments subsidise clean energy, the transition away from fossil fuels is likely to accelerate.
Task 2 (second + hedge): If education were entirely free, access might improve, though the burden on public finances would probably be considerable.
Speaking Part 3: It tends to depend on the context, but on the whole I'd say technology has made communication easier.
End of Chapter 7, and of Module 2. Module 3 (Band 9.0 Masterclass), Chapter 8 follows.

title: 7. Practice · Conditionals, Hedging & Hypothetical Reasoning
group: Module 2 · Band 7.0+ Complex Structures & Range Booster
blocks: The four conditionals sit on a scale of reality, from always-true to no-longer-possible. Choosing the right one is choosing how real you want your claim to sound -- get this wrong and a genuine possibility reads as pure fantasy, or vice versa.
**Why it matters:** Conditional choice signals how confident you are in a claim, which matters enormously in Task 2 argumentation.
The four conditionals, as a scale of reality
**Zero** -- general truth / scientific fact: If you heat ice, it melts.
**First** -- a real, likely future possibility: If taxes rise, consumption will fall.
**Third** -- impossible now, because the moment has passed.
Read the scale in order: zero is always true, first is realistically possible, second is imagined, third is impossible.
Formal English uses **were** for all subjects in the second conditional -- If the government were to act... -- and this is the safer choice in Writing.

blocks.title: Exercise 7.1 · Conditional Rewrite
blocks.instructions: Put the verb in brackets into the correct form for the conditional required, or rewrite as instructed. Watch the if-clause: no “will” or “would” there.

items.prompt: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it ______ (boil).
accepted: boils
items.reason: Zero conditional: general truth, present simple in both clauses.

items.prompt: If the government reduces tuition fees, more students ______ (enrol).
accepted: will enrol
items.reason: First conditional: a real future possibility.

items.prompt: If I ______ (be) the mayor, I would ban private cars in the centre.
accepted: were

items.prompt: If they had listened to the experts, the disaster ______ (avoid).
accepted: would have been avoided
items.reason: Third conditional: past perfect + would have + past participle (passive).

items.prompt: If the price of oil rises, transport costs ______ (increase).
accepted: will increase

items.prompt: If people recycled more, landfill sites ______ (fill) up less quickly.
accepted: would fill

items.prompt: If the company had invested in training, its staff ______ (be) more productive today. (mixed)
accepted: would be
items.reason: Mixed conditional: past condition, present result.

items.prompt: Ice melts if the temperature ______ (rise) above zero.
accepted: rises

items.prompt: If more people ______ (use) public transport, the air would be cleaner.
accepted: used
items.reason: Second conditional: past simple in the if-clause.

items.prompt: If the trend continues, sea levels ______ (rise) by a metre this century.
accepted: will rise

items.prompt: If governments ______ (act) sooner, many species would not have become extinct.
accepted: had acted
items.reason: Third conditional: past perfect in the if-clause.

items.prompt: If I were you, I ______ (choose) the science course.
accepted: would choose

items.prompt: Rewrite as an inverted conditional: If the authorities had responded quickly, lives would have been saved.
items.answer: Had the authorities responded quickly, lives would have been saved.
accepted: Had the authorities responded quickly, lives would have been saved.

items.prompt: If children ______ (not / get) enough sleep, their concentration suffers.
accepted: do not get
don't get

items.prompt: If renewable energy became cheaper, developing countries ______ (adopt) it faster.
accepted: would adopt

blocks: Band 5 writing is full of absolutes -- always, never, everyone. Band 8 writing hedges its claims with modals and tendency verbs, which paradoxically makes them sound more credible, not less confident.
**Why it matters:** Hedging is one of the fastest, most learnable upgrades from Band 6-7 writing into Band 8 writing -- it's a toolkit, not a talent.
Hedging softens a claim so it isn't an absolute statement. "Immigration boosts the economy" is a claim you can't fully prove; "Immigration can boost the economy" is one you can defend.
**Modal verbs of possibility:** may, might, could, can.
**Verbs of tendency:** tend to, be likely to, appear to, seem to.
**Adverbs of frequency/degree:** often, generally, in many cases, to some extent, relatively.
**Impersonal frames:** it is often argued that, it could be said that.
Hedging is not weakness or vagueness -- it's precision about how certain you actually are.

blocks.title: Exercise 7.2 · Hedging Upgrade Drill
blocks.instructions: Each sentence is overstated. Rewrite it with appropriate hedging so that it sounds measured and academic.

items.prompt: Fast food always causes serious health problems.
items.answer: Fast food can cause serious health problems.
accepted: Fast food can cause serious health problems.
Fast food may cause serious health problems.
Fast food often causes serious health problems.

items.prompt: Everyone agrees that social media is harmful.
items.answer: Many people argue that social media can be harmful.
accepted: Many people argue that social media can be harmful.
It is often argued that social media can be harmful.
items.reason: Replace the universal “everyone … is” with a hedged claim.

items.prompt: Immigration will definitely boost the economy.
items.answer: Immigration is likely to boost the economy.
accepted: Immigration is likely to boost the economy.
Immigration can boost the economy.

items.prompt: Students who study abroad always become more independent.
items.answer: Students who study abroad tend to become more independent.
accepted: Students who study abroad tend to become more independent.

items.prompt: Technology never has any negative effects.
items.answer: Technology does not always have negative effects.
accepted: Technology does not always have negative effects.
Technology rarely has serious negative effects.

items.prompt: All young people prefer texting to phone calls.
items.answer: The majority of young people appear to prefer texting to phone calls.
accepted: The majority of young people appear to prefer texting to phone calls.
Many young people seem to prefer texting to phone calls.
items.reason: Replace “all … prefer” with a quantifier + hedge.

items.prompt: Higher taxes will completely solve the problem of pollution.
items.answer: Higher taxes may help to reduce pollution.
accepted: Higher taxes may help to reduce pollution.
Higher taxes could help to reduce pollution.

items.prompt: Every developed country has excellent public services.
items.answer: Most developed countries tend to have good public services.
accepted: Most developed countries tend to have good public services.

items.prompt: Working from home is always more productive than working in an office.
items.answer: Working from home can be more productive than working in an office.
accepted: Working from home can be more productive than working in an office.

items.prompt: Tourism completely destroys local culture.
items.answer: Tourism may, to some extent, erode local culture.
accepted: Tourism may, to some extent, erode local culture.
Tourism can erode local culture to some extent.
